name: Streetscore: Which Place Looks Safer? (New York, Boston)
description:
Method replication: the same pairwise safety question as the data behind the paper; the images are not the paper's stimuli (new Google Street View views of New York and Boston, © Google). Naik, Philipoom, Raskar & Hidalgo (2014, IEEE CVPR Workshops) trained Streetscore, an algorithm that predicts the perceived safety of a streetscape, on pairwise votes from an online survey with more than 7,000 participants (Place Pulse). Geometric texton and colour histograms with GIST predicted safety best, and Streetscore then mapped perceived safety for about one million Google Street View images in 21 US cities.

What participants do: after consent, 20 pairs of street views from New York and Boston, drawn at random from 94; for each pair they click the place that looks safer. Then age and gender.

Analysis as in the paper: TrueSkill rating per image from the pairwise votes, rescaled to 0–10, then image features (colour, texture, GIST or modern deep features) regressed on the scores.

Differences from the original study: (1) the images are new Google Street View views (2016–2026) from random points in New York (29) and Boston (65), not the Place Pulse set; (2) the online survey allowed unlimited votes, this template asks 20 pairs; (3) the earlier version of this template added optional 1–10 single-image ratings, which are removed here because they were not in the paper. The earlier version showed 12 photographs cropped from the paper PDF.
